name: Gull
lede: Gull is an old English word for a shade of grey, now shown as a grayish olive; the books say little about it, but one nineteenth-century color chart took several of its whites and greys from gull feathers.

sections.title: An old name for grey
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary glosses *gull* as an ancient word for a grey tone [1]. The Maerz and Paul *Dictionary of Color* of 1930 lists it on plate 38 and dates its first use to about 1350 [2]. Which gull the name first pointed to is undocumented in the books we hold, and so is who coined it [1].

sections.title: The swatch is not a gull's grey
sections.body:
The swatch here is the Maerz and Paul color as the library carries it [2]. It sits closest to the ISCC-NBS block called grayish olive [2]. That is far darker and greener than the plumage of a gull, whose back the Werner chart reads as a pale grey [3]. The old word and the modern swatch have drifted apart.

Its nearest named neighbors are [[beetle]], [[bronze-lustre]] and [[greenish-hunter-green]] [2]. Of the greys, [[grey]] is the parent word, and the browner [[olive-brown]] is nearer in hue.

sections.title: Gulls on Werner's chart
sections.body:
Gulls do appear in the color record, just not under this name. Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, in the Syme edition that Baty reproduces, picked its example for each color from birds, flowers and minerals [3]. The back of the black-headed gull stands for Pearl Grey, its breast for Snow White, and its head for Broccoli Brown [3][4][5]. The kittiwake supplies Greyish White and, at the junction of neck and back, Purplish White [3][6].

The chart treats the gull as a bird of whites and pale greys. Nothing in it points to the olive the word now shows on screen.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color, this dark olive is common: it appears in 2,246 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 9.44 per cent, as photographed [7]. The more cautious within-painting lens finds it in 1,345 [7]. Its peak is the 1700s, at 8.0 per cent of the 3,449 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the baseline of the same museums [7]. Most often it plays a hidden color, by lightness rank within the painting, in 31 per cent of those 1,345 [7].

The most devoted painter is [[painter:peter-snayers|Peter Snayers]], in 8 of his 16 works here, 6.9 times the baseline [7]. It travels with [[kronberg-s-green]] and [[courge-green]] more than chance would suggest [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test, and the name's earliest record in our sources (1930) is far later than the first match in the archive [7].
